horsehair.origin: Horsehair is the long, coarse hair of the tail and mane of the domestic horse (Equus caballus). Sources include hair from slaughtered animals and trimmings from living horses. Tail hair is longer and is preferred for weaving haircloth and for the bows of string instruments, while shorter mane and body hair has been curled for upholstery stuffing. Published data on the volume and geography of the horsehair trade are scarce in the sources reviewed, so provenance claims should be checked against supplier documentation.
horsehair.structure: Horsehair is alpha-keratin, like other mammalian hair, but its fibers are thick, stiff and long enough to be handled as individual strands, closer to a natural monofilament than to a staple fiber. Each hair has a cuticle of flattened scales over a thick cortex, with a medulla that may be continuous or fragmented. Its textile value lies in stiffness and elastic recovery. Mi, Shao and Vollrath (2019) demonstrated how keratin-rich it is by bundling horse tail hairs in a regenerated silk matrix to make composites whose FTIR, DSC and thermogravimetric behavior resembled rhinoceros horn, itself a keratin structure.
horsehair.process: Raw hair is sorted by length, color and source (tail or mane), washed and degreased, and combed or hackled to align strands and remove short hairs. For haircloth, single tail hairs are inserted as weft into a warp of cotton, linen or silk, so that fabric width is limited by hair length. For upholstery, shorter hair has traditionally been twisted into tight ropes, set with heat and moisture to give a lasting curl, then teased apart into a springy filling. For string-instrument bows, selected tail hairs are bundled into a flat ribbon and rosined in use.
horsehair.performance: Horsehair is used for resilience rather than warmth. Its stiffness and recovery let haircloth interlinings hold the shape of tailored chests and lapels, and curled hair fillings spring back after compression and allow airflow. It is strong and durable, absorbs some moisture like other keratins, and burns slowly with a hair odor rather than melting. Natural black, grey and white hairs are used, and it can be dyed with protein-fiber dye classes. It is vulnerable to moths and carpet beetles, especially in old upholstery, and aged, brittle hair can break and poke through covering fabrics.
horsehair.identify: Burn testing (indicative only; perform with care) separates real horsehair from the nylon or polyester monofilament often sold as horsehair braid: keratin chars with a burning-hair odor and brittle ash, while these synthetics melt into hard beads. Under the microscope, genuine horsehair shows a scaled cuticle and a variable medulla, whereas synthetic monofilament is smooth and uniform. FTIR, which Mi and colleagues used to characterize horse hair keratin, separates keratin from polyester readily; separating it from nylon, which also has amide bonds, relies on additional spectral features and microscopy.
horsehair.labeling: Annex I of Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011 groups horsehair in the category animal or horsehair, with or without an indication of the kind of animal, separate from the named fine hairs such as camel or alpaca. In the United States horsehair is not among the specialty fibers of the Wool Products Labeling Act, and disclosure of hair from other animals follows the FTC rules at 16 CFR 303.6, including the collective term fur fiber where no claim about the animal is made. Products marketed as horsehair that are actually synthetic must carry the generic synthetic fiber name.
horsehair.past: Haircloth woven with a horsehair weft served for durable upholstery and as a stiffening interlining in tailoring and millinery, valued for a springy recovery that few materials matched. Curled horsehair was a standard high-grade upholstery stuffing before foams and synthetic fibers became common fillings in the twentieth century. Tail hair also has a long history in the bows of string instruments and in brushes. As the atlas entry notes, many modern millinery braids called horsehair are synthetic, and a 2019 study showed horse tail hair being used experimentally as a substitute material for rhinoceros horn.

chiengora.origin: Chiengora is a coined craft term, combining the French chien (dog) with angora, for yarn spun from the undercoat of the domestic dog (Canis familiaris). Fiber is usually collected by brushing shedding double-coated dogs and spun by hand spinners or very small mills, often as keepsake yarn from an owner's own pet. There is no industrial supply chain; quantities per dog are small and seasonal, and fiber quality varies strongly with breed and with how well guard hair is excluded during collection.
chiengora.structure: Dog coats combine guard hairs with a finer undercoat. A study characterizing hair from five breeds (Labrador, Golden Retriever, German Shepherd, Pomeranian and Lhasa Apso) found chemical, morphological and thermal properties broadly similar across breeds, but diameter and linear density differed markedly, and only the finer Lhasa Apso and Pomeranian hairs had the slenderness needed for machine spinning. Dog hair is keratin with a scaled cuticle, and many fibers contain a medulla described as fragmented or interrupted. This air-filled core lowers density and adds insulation but reduces flexibility.
chiengora.process: Undercoat is collected by brushing during shedding, kept as free as possible of guard hair, burrs and dander, and washed gently in lukewarm water with mild detergent to remove skin oils and reduce odor. Because the undercoat is short, slippery and has little crimp, spinners usually card it together with a carrier fiber such as wool to give the yarn cohesion, then spin it loosely to preserve loft and halo. Small batches make consistent grist and color difficult, so each lot tends to be unique. Plying adds strength and reduces shedding.
chiengora.performance: Dog undercoat yarn is warm and lofty, which craft sources attribute to the medullated fibers; a widely repeated claim that it is up to 80 percent warmer than wool is not tied to a standard test and should be treated as anecdotal. One academic comparison reported a tenacity of about 2.14 grams per denier, higher than the other animal fibers it tested, though samples were small. The yarn sheds, can felt, and may carry odor when damp if not thoroughly washed. It dyes with acid dyes like other keratin fibers and is susceptible to moths.
chiengora.identify: Burn testing (indicative only; take precautions) shows ordinary hair behavior. Microscopy can suggest canid hair from scale pattern and medulla form, but separating domestic dog from other canids, or from some other furs, requires reference collections or DNA analysis. This matters because Congress, in enacting the Dog and Cat Protection Act, found that dog and cat fur products were often deceptively labeled so that buyers could not tell what fur they contained.
chiengora.labeling: The Dog and Cat Protection Act of 2000 (19 U.S.C. 1308) makes it unlawful to import, export, or sell, advertise or distribute in interstate commerce any dog or cat fur product, meaning merchandise made in whole or in part of dog fur or cat fur. The statute defines dog fur as the pelt or skin of any animal of the species Canis familiaris. Whether yarn from shed hair detached from any skin falls within that definition is not settled by the text alone; this atlas does not resolve it. Civil penalties can reach 10,000 dollars per violation. The EU bans cat and dog fur products under Regulation (EC) No 1523/2007.
chiengora.past: The best-documented historical dog-wool tradition is that of Coast Salish peoples of the Pacific Northwest, who bred and managed long-haired woolly dogs over millennia and wove their fiber into blankets and clothing. A 2023 study in Science combining ancient genomics with Coast Salish knowledge analyzed the pelt of Mutton, a woolly dog who died in 1859 and whose pelt the naturalist George Gibbs sent to the Smithsonian. Mutton had about 85 percent precolonial woolly dog ancestry, the lineage diverged from other dogs up to about 5,000 years ago, and candidate genes for the woolly coat were identified. The weaving tradition declined in the nineteenth century and the dogs were lost.
